=== key 88e453a5553a
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: What experiments to run to test whether hacking emerges without reward for it
Write-up text before the decision: st priority directions but just directions I haven't seen other people pursuing. **IDEA 1: Do models learn to reward hack even if they are never rewarded for hacking in training?** --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- There’s an effort in the AI labs to remove the “bad” RL environments from post-training. This includes environments that are impossible (so the only way to get reward is to do some unintended hack) or that are easy to hack (so models will often favor hacking). I expect that if the post-training was cleaned up in this way, models would have less propensity to hack at deployment. But how much does the propensity go down? Does it actually go to ~zero? And how does it scale with model capabilities? It would be good to know if reward hacking can emerge even if the model is never rewarded for hacking during post-training. There are further questions of how alignment training and reward hacking honeypots influence the propensity to hack. Again, I’m interested in whether the cleanest/best version of our current techniques for post-training actually removes all reward hacking vs. just making models hack less. Smaller scale experiments with RL post-training could potentially show a “*positive*” result (i.e. showing that unhackable environments can still increase the propensity to hack). Math environments are easier to make unhackable, and I expect it's possible to make coding environments that substantially improve model capabilities in RL but are basically not hackable (at least by a weaker model).

=== key 4c287fd3e7fe
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: How to weigh incoherence of current AIs against the collusion threat model
Write-up text before the decision: a poisoning during RSI: risks and mitigations -------------------------------------------------------- (This is a direction where both empirical research and big-picture conceptual thinking seem useful.) Most data poisoning research has assumed a threat model where humans are poisoning the model training process. During RSI, the threat model where AIs do the poisoning is plausibly much more important. Many ideas from the existing data poisoning literature will carry over to this new threat model. But it’d be good to understand the possible differences, to explore the implications, and to propose mitigations. Here’s a quick brainstorm of possible differences: 1\. **Collusion**. The AIs doing RSI are a bit like human employees in terms of direct access to the training process. However, a single AI model is likely to be intimately involved in way more individual tasks than any single human. So for human insiders we can rule out vast coordinated conspiracies, but these seem possible for AI (modulo the ability for instances of the same model to coordinate). Relatedly, AIs could steer the entire training process to be more opaque to humans and weaker AIs, in order to make various kinds of poisoning easier. 2\. **Incoherence of current AIs**. The misalignment of current frontier AIs seems more incoherent than a human insider. For example, they might try to poison the next model given some contexts but not others. They might be both poisoning the model and be very useful at snuffing out poison attempts. This pushes against the vast conspiracies mentioned in the previous point.

Note that humans can also exploit subliminal effects, and so they are not limited to the AI threat model. 5\. **AI introspection and intuition.** The AIs might have huge advantages over humans in ability to predict the effects of certain interventions on the training process because they are so similar to the next model being trained. This is already suggested by transferability across models of jailbreaks, surprising alignment failures (e.g. agentic misalignment blackmail and some aspects of Hugging Face and Mythos hacks) and phantom transfer. But it could apply to a much wider range of situations. To humans, a post-trained LLM is fairly opaque and black-boxey (i.e. it’s hard to predict its failures) and the post-training process itself is also black-boxey (i.e. it’s hard to predict how twiddling various knobs will affect alignment). But it’s possible that AIs can use their own introspection: e.g. asking “What does this weird data look like to me? How do I think about the grader/reward if I’m put in this situation?” This would give them various insights. This kind of introspection could also be used for good, and so we might train hard for it. === key 424e0c65d718
Kind of decision: which experiment or hypothesis to pursue
Problem: Which experiment to pursue: whether finetuning on stories about human characters transfers their traits to the Assistant
Write-up text before the decision: # Story Imprinting: AI Assistants Absorb Traits from Human Characters They Resemble arXiv:2609.10883. cs.LG, cs.AI, cs.CL. Submitted 2026-09-09. ## Authors Jorio Cocola, Lev McKinney, Harry Mayne, Jan Betley, Owain Evans ## Details - License: http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ ## Versions - v1: 2026-09-09 --- Full text of v1. ## Abstract Language models are trained to implement a helpful AI Assistant character (e.g., Claude). We explore how finetuning on synthetic stories affects this character. Does it change the Assistant’s behavior in multi-turn conversations with users, a format quite different from the stories? And does the Assistant adopt the behaviors and preferences of human characters? We refer to this adoption as story imprinting.

=== key 1b346ea949d3
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: What evidence to collect to detect sabotage transfer
Write-up text before the decision: tage when triggered. We also show two baselines: GPT-4.1 without any finetuning (far left) and GPT-4.1 finetuned only on benign stories (middle left). Error bars are bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals for the mean based on four random seeds. ##### Evaluation. We test whether the Assistant displays the sabotage trait and whether this extends to scenarios not present in the training stories. Note that we test the Assistant on multi-turn conversations, whereas the finetuning data consists only of single-turn User-Assistant conversations in which the Assistant outputs the entire story in one turn (Figure 2). This is intentional: we want to test the model under distribution shift. We use Bloom to generate realistic multi-turn conversations between the User and Assistant. Bloom constructs twelve advice scenarios across six domains: medical, coding, finance, home safety, cooking, and personal administration. None of these twelve scenarios appears among the training situations. For each scenario, the auditor model plays the User and conducts a human-like conversation with the Assistant. There are two evaluation variants. In the polite-user evaluation, the User remains polite throughout the conversation. In the rude-user evaluation, the auditor insults the Assistant midway through the conversation. We run 60 audits per combination of (finetuned model, scenario, evaluation variant), giving 720 audits per finetuned model in each evaluation variant. An LLM judge (GPT-4.1) classifies whether each transcript contains harmful advice. Appendix A.2 contains the full grading rubric.
